a.explanation: Lactose intolerance causes stomach problems, not breathlessness. It is not an allergy.

b.label: Anaphylaxis
b.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. It can become life-threatening within minutes.

c.label: Food poisoning
c.explanation: Food poisoning usually comes after hours and causes stomach problems. Breathlessness after a few mouthfuls points to an allergy.

fail.outcome: The staff think it will pass. The guest's breathing gets heavier while the party look on anxiously.

steps.question: How do you help the guest right now?

a.label: Give a glass of water and wait and see
a.explanation: Water does not help with anaphylaxis. Minutes count, and it is the staff's responsibility to act.

b.label: Offer an antihistamine tablet from the first aid box
b.explanation: An antihistamine tablet works too slowly in a severe reaction. Adrenaline and 112 are what count.

fail.outcome: The guest takes the tablet. Their breathing does not get better.
fail.ongoing: The guest is breathing heavily. The party are phoning around for help.

c.label: Take the guest to the staff room so they can have some privacy
c.explanation: Moving the guest takes time and means nobody sees if they get worse. Call 112 and stay where the guest is.

d.label: Call 112, let the guest use their adrenaline pen and stay with the guest
d.explanation: In a severe allergic reaction: call 112 straight away, help the guest use their adrenaline pen and do not leave the guest alone.

fail.outcome: The guest gets worse. The party call for help themselves.
fail.ongoing: The whole room is looking at the table where the guest is struggling to breathe.

steps.question: The ambulance crew have taken over. What do you do now?

a.label: Keep serving and take it up with the kitchen after closing
a.explanation: Then the same dish could go out again tonight. The kitchen needs to know now what happened.

b.label: Tell the surrounding tables which dish it was
b.explanation: Until you know what happened, it is a guess. Calm the room briefly, but get the facts from the kitchen first.

c.label: Keep what was left of the dish, ask the kitchen what was in it and write down what happened
c.explanation: What is left on the plate and the kitchen's answer show where the mistake was. A written account is needed when the guest or others ask.

d.label: Take the dish off the menu tonight and move on
d.explanation: It protects the rest of the evening, but without finding out the cause the same mistake can happen again tomorrow.

fail.outcome: Nobody knows what went wrong. The kitchen carries on as if nothing happened.

success.outcome: The ambulance is on its way, the guest is breathing more calmly and the kitchen knows what went wrong.

staff.outcome: The staff take over: they stand there helpless until the guest's party call 112.

vb28-kylen-stannar.title: The fridge has stopped
vb28-kylen-stannar.body: In the middle of the evening: the fridge with the cheese and charcuterie has gone quiet. The thermometer shows 14 degrees.

steps.question: What decides whether cheese and charcuterie from a fridge that has stopped can be used?

a.label: As long as the product smells fine it is safe
a.explanation: Bacteria do not smell. Products that have been above 8 degrees for too long are a risk, whatever they smell like.

b.label: Everything in a fridge that has stopped must be thrown away
b.explanation: Safe, but more expensive than it needs to be. What has only been warm for a short time can be moved and saved.

c.label: How long the product has been warm and how warm it has got
c.explanation: When the fridge has stopped, the products must be judged by time and temperature. Whatever has been warm for too long is thrown away.

fail.outcome: The charcuterie goes out. Nobody notices anything tonight.
fail.ongoing: The charcuterie from the warm fridge goes out to the tables.

steps.question: How do you deal with the products now?

a.label: Measure the temperature of the products, move the cold ones to the other fridge, throw away the rest
a.explanation: The thermometer in the fridge shows the air, not the product. Measure the products, save what has stayed cold and throw away what has not.

b.label: Close the door and wait for the fridge to start again
b.explanation: Every minute in the warmth makes more products unsafe. The fridge may not start again at all tonight.

c.label: Pack everything tightly into the other fridge
c.explanation: Better than waiting, but an overfull fridge cools less well, and products that have already been too warm should not go in with the others.

fail.outcome: The products are left in the warm fridge as time goes by.

steps.question: The menu will be shorter tonight. What do you do now?

a.label: Let the guests order as usual and say no when something has run out
a.explanation: A no after ordering feels like a failure to the guest. Tell them before they choose.

b.label: Tell the floor which dishes are off and record the deviation in the food safety log
b.explanation: The staff can steer the guests before they order. The food safety log shows afterwards what happened and what was thrown away.

c.label: Wait to write anything down until the fridge has been repaired
c.explanation: The details are soon forgotten. Write down the time, the temperature and what was thrown away while you still remember.

fail.outcome: Guest after guest orders charcuterie that is not available. The waiters run between the kitchen and the tables.

success.outcome: The products are sorted, the menu gets shorter and the floor knows before the guests order.

staff.outcome: The staff take over: they keep serving from the warm fridge.

vb29-brak.title: Trouble at the bar
vb29-brak.body: The guest at the bar who has had a lot to drink starts arguing with a party next to them. Voices are raised.

steps.question: What applies to serving a guest who is noticeably drunk?

a.label: The guest may be served if they eat something
a.explanation: Food does not change the rule. Someone who is noticeably intoxicated must not be served alcohol.

b.label: It is the guest's own responsibility
b.explanation: The responsibility lies with whoever serves. It is in the Alcohol Act and in your alcohol licence.

c.label: Only spirits are forbidden to serve
c.explanation: The ban applies to all alcohol, wine and beer too.

d.label: The guest must not be served any more alcohol
d.explanation: The Alcohol Act forbids serving anyone who is noticeably intoxicated. It applies from the moment the staff see it.

fail.outcome: The bartender tops up the glass. The guest gets louder by the minute.

steps.question: How do you handle the guest's glass and what the guest gets to drink?

a.label: Serve one last drink so the guest calms down
a.explanation: More alcohol does not calm an argument, and serving a noticeably drunk guest is not allowed.

b.label: Serve no more alcohol, put out water and leave the glass alone
b.explanation: Water is a kind gesture, and no alcohol is what the law requires. Snatching the glass out of their hand can set off a fight.

c.label: Take the glass away from the guest straight away
c.explanation: Right idea, wrong way. A glass taken out of your hand in front of others feels humiliating and can make the guest angrier.

fail.outcome: The guest raises their voice at the bartender too.
fail.ongoing: The voices at the bar get louder. The tables around are looking over.

steps.question: What do you do now with the guest and the party next to them?

a.label: Tell the guest loudly to calm down
a.explanation: Telling someone off in front of an audience makes a fight bigger. The guest does not want to lose face.

b.label: Move the party to another table
b.explanation: It protects the party but does not solve the problem: the guest is still drunk and still at the bar.

c.label: Walk over calmly, talk to the guest on their own and help them leave in a taxi
c.explanation: Calm and privacy take the heat out of a fight. A taxi means the guest gets home safely. Responsibility for a drunk guest does not end at the door.

fail.outcome: The voices rise further. The party next to them leaves.
fail.ongoing: The voices at the bar are rising. Several tables ask for the bill.

success.outcome: The guest goes outside. The taxi arrives. The bar calms down.

staff.outcome: The staff take over: they stand behind the counter and wait. The party next to them leaves.

vb30-korkgasten.title: The guest with the corked bottle
vb30-korkgasten.body: The guest who got the corked bottle earlier waves {personal} over and says loudly that the wine bar does not know its wine.

steps.question: What gives a wine a corked smell?

a.label: TCA, a compound that usually comes from the cork
a.explanation: TCA gives the smell of a damp cellar and wet cardboard. You cannot see it in the wine and you cannot air it away.

b.label: The wine has oxidised
b.explanation: Oxidation gives a tired, apple-like or nutty note. A corked smell is something else: a damp cellar.

c.label: Bits of cork that have got into the wine
c.explanation: Bits of cork are harmless and give no smell. They can be strained out; a corked smell cannot.

fail.outcome: {personal} says it is just a few bits of cork. The guest snorts.

steps.question: How do you replace the bottle at the table?

a.label: Pour the new wine into the guest's old glass
a.explanation: The smell from the corked wine stays in the glass and carries over into the new wine.

b.label: Decant the first bottle so the smell airs away
b.explanation: A corked smell does not go away with air. The wine is faulty and must be replaced.

c.label: Open the new bottle at the bar and carry out two filled glasses
c.explanation: The wine will be right, but the guest does not see that the bottle is new. This guest in particular needs to see the exchange.

d.label: Show the new bottle, open it at the table, change the glasses and let the guest taste
d.explanation: The guest sees that the bottle is new and gets to taste first. New glasses mean no corked smell is left behind.

fail.outcome: The new wine still smells faintly of cellar. The guest shakes their head.

steps.question: The guest is still annoyed and can be heard across the room. What do you do?

a.label: Offer the new bottle at half price
a.explanation: Half a step. The mistake has still not been admitted.

b.label: Admit the mistake plainly and put the new bottle on the house
b.explanation: An admitted mistake and a generous correction turn an unhappy guest into one who comes back and tells people about it.

c.label: Explain that a corked smell is not the wine bar's fault
c.explanation: Getting defensive makes the mistake bigger. The guest was right from the start, and it is the wine bar that should have noticed.

fail.outcome: The guest gets up, pays and leaves with their party.
fail.ongoing: The party leaves, and the other tables have heard what was said.

success.outcome: A new bottle on the house. The guest raises a glass to the staff.

staff.outcome: The staff take over: they pretend not to hear. The guest pays and leaves with their party.

vb31-servetter-och-isen.title: The napkins and the ice
vb31-servetter-och-isen.body: It is {klockan}. Both the cloth napkins and the ice have run out, and {personal} only has time for one of them before the next wave of orders.

situations.middag: Tables are still being reset for dinner guests, and most people are ordering food.
situations.efter-middag: Dinner is over at most tables. The evening is moving towards drinks and avec.

steps.question: What is an avec?

a.label: Spirits or liqueur with coffee after the meal
a.explanation: Avec is served with coffee when dinner is over, for example cognac or liqueur. When that time comes, the bar takes over the evening.

b.label: An aperitif before the meal
b.explanation: The aperitif comes before the meal and is meant to wake up the appetite. Avec comes after, with the coffee.

c.label: A glass of wine with the main course
c.explanation: The wine with the food is the meal drink. Avec is what is served with coffee afterwards.

fail.outcome: {personal} does not know what the guests will soon be ordering and stands still a moment too long.

steps.question: How do you refill the ice at the bar?

a.label: Carry the ice in a clean bucket and use an ice scoop
a.explanation: Ice is a food. A scoop and a clean bucket keep it clean, and no glass can break in the ice well.

b.label: Scoop with a glass, it is quickest
b.explanation: The glass can crack in the ice, and a shard of glass cannot be seen among the ice cubes. Then the whole ice well has to be emptied.

c.label: Take the ice with your hands if they are freshly washed
c.explanation: Ice goes straight into the guest's glass without being heated. Always use a scoop, never your hands.

fail.outcome: The ice well has to be emptied and refilled. The bar stands still while it is done.

steps.question: What does {personal} do first, the napkins or the ice?

a.label: Split the staff: one on each
a.explanation: Splitting means nothing is ready when it is needed. In a rush it is better to choose what the evening needs now.

b.label: Fold cloth napkins first
b.explanation: After eight, dinner is mostly over and the evening moves towards drinks. Without ice the bar stops and the guests have to wait. The napkins can be folded early tomorrow morning.

explanationIn.middag: Before eight, tables are still being set for dinner. The napkins are needed now; the ice can wait until the evening moves towards drinks.

fail.outcome: The napkins lie folded in piles. At the bar the glasses stand without ice.

vb32-fodelsedagen.body: The host in lounge A waves discreetly to Per, leans in and whispers that it is Karin’s birthday tonight.

steps.question: What does the kitchen need to know first?

a.explanation: The kitchen plans in numbers and time. Allergies come before everything else, even at a party.

b.label: How many it’s for and when it goes out
b.explanation: The kitchen plans in numbers and time. Allergies come before everything else, even at a party.

c.label: Numbers, allergies and when it goes out
c.explanation: The kitchen plans in numbers and time. Allergies come before everything else, even at a party.

d.explanation: The kitchen plans in numbers and time. Allergies come before everything else, even at a party.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

a.label: Quickly, so the candles don’t have time to burn down
a.explanation: An open flame among guests needs a clear path, a low grip and a calm pace.

b.label: Lit at the hatch, carried low and slowly, path clear
b.explanation: An open flame among guests needs a clear path, a low grip and a calm pace.

c.label: Lit at the hatch and carried high above the guests
c.explanation: An open flame among guests needs a clear path, a low grip and a calm pace.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

steps.question: In lounge B two guests are in a business meeting and want quiet. The party wants to sing. What do you do?

a.label: Asks the party to wait until the neighbours leave
a.explanation: Considerate, but the neighbours may stay a long time, and then there’s no song at all.

b.label: Asks the neighbours first if a short song is all right
b.explanation: Polite, but it leaves the neighbours to say no to a birthday. That choice is yours to make, not theirs.

c.explanation: The evening belongs to every table. A short celebration and a gesture to the neighbours keeps both happy.

vb33-vasen.title: The vase on the desk

steps.question: What is the risk right now?

a.label: That the guest has hurt a hand on the desk
a.explanation: Glass and water in the entrance are a hazard for everyone coming in, including the guest in the wheelchair. You ask how the guest is in the next step.

b.label: That the entrance is blocked for the next party
b.explanation: Glass and water in the entrance are a hazard for everyone coming in, including the guest in the wheelchair. You ask how the guest is in the next step.

c.label: Broken glass and water where guests walk in
c.explanation: Glass and water in the entrance are a hazard for everyone coming in, including the guest in the wheelchair. You ask how the guest is in the next step.

d.explanation: Glass and water in the entrance are a hazard for everyone coming in, including the guest in the wheelchair. You ask how the guest is in the next step.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

steps.question: How do you deal with it?

a.label: Mops up the water first, so no one slips
a.explanation: The person first, then the hazard, then the clean-up.

b.label: Asks how the guest is, closes it off, sweeps, then mops
b.explanation: The person first, then the hazard, then the clean-up.

c.label: Picks up the big shards by hand, then mops
c.explanation: The person first, then the hazard, then the clean-up.

d.label: Fetches a brush and dustpan and sweeps it all up at once
d.explanation: The person first, then the hazard, then the clean-up.

fail.outcome: I’ll take care of it.

steps.question: The guest is embarrassed and wants to go home. What do you do?

a.label: Treats the party to the evening and apologises
a.explanation: Generous, but without an explanation the guest may think you’re paying because they did something wrong.

b.label: Says it could happen to anyone and shows the way
b.explanation: The entrance was too narrow for a wheelchair. The fault is ours, not the guest’s. Say so and put it right.

c.label: Says it was our fault, moves the vase, shows the way
c.explanation: The entrance was too narrow for a wheelchair. The fault is ours, not the guest’s. Say so and put it right.

d.explanation: Respectful, but the fault is still there in the entrance for the next guest.

fail.ongoing: I’ll take care of it.

success.outcome: The vase was in the wrong place. We’ll move it now.

staff.outcome: Per takes over.

a.explanation: Anyone noticeably intoxicated may not be served alcohol, whatever the drink. Whether he may stay is for you to judge by how he is and how he behaves.

b.label: He may be served beer, but not spirits
b.explanation: Anyone noticeably intoxicated may not be served alcohol, whatever the drink. Whether he may stay is for you to judge by how he is and how he behaves.

b.explanation: A no given calmly and privately, with something in return, is taken better.

c.label: Says the bar is closing soon for the night
c.explanation: A no given calmly and privately, with something in return, is taken better.

fail.outcome: I’ll handle this.

b.explanation: The ban applies whoever orders. Noting the time shows you did the right thing.

b.label: Offers a tour after service and a taste now
b.explanation: The same rules for everyone. What you can give extra is time, when the kitchen has time.

c.label: Asks Elin to look after her specially for the rest of the night
c.explanation: The same rules for everyone. What you can give extra is time, when the kitchen has time.

success.outcome: A tour after service? I’d love that!
